analysis.one_liner: Funds a full modernization of America's public housing into energy-efficient, zero-carbon homes with resident jobs and training.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in August 2026 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, where it has sat with no further action and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Green New Deal for Public Housing Act would give housing agencies federal grants to rehabilitate and modernize all of America's public housing — new insulation, heat pumps, electric appliances, solar panels, clean water pipes, and repairs — with the goal of making every unit a zero-carbon home within ten years of receiving money. It would require that a growing share of the construction jobs and contracts go to public housing residents and resident-owned businesses, set prevailing-wage and apprenticeship rules for contractors, and repeal the 1998 Faircloth Amendment that bans building new public housing. It also gives residents new formal power, including elected resident councils and signed resident approval of funding applications.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 1.5 million people living in public housing, mostly very low-income families, seniors, and people with disabilities, would get renovated, healthier, cheaper-to-run homes, plus training and hiring preferences for the jobs the repairs create. Workers in the building trades would gain a large supply of prevailing-wage work.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Public housing residents and building-trades workers

how_it_helps.text: Provides grants for deep energy retrofits: insulation, heat pumps, all-electric appliances, efficient windows, and repairs to bring units up to federal, state, and local building codes.
Requires replacement of lead, PFAS, arsenic, and copper-contaminated water pipes when testing exceeds strict EPA thresholds, directly addressing tainted drinking water in aging developments.
Funds community resilience features: battery backup for at least 48 hours of power in emergencies, solar panels, community energy generation, and 100Mbps public internet for residents.
Creates workforce development grants tied to registered apprenticeships, with $250 weekly stipends, childcare, and reserved training slots for formerly incarcerated local residents.
Requires an escalating share of jobs (up to 90%) and contracts (up to 50%) to go to low-income residents and resident-owned businesses under the Section 3 program.
Requires prevailing wages under the Davis-Bacon Act, allows union recognition where a majority of workers join, and bans temporary-staffing hiring except in certified emergencies.
Repeals the Faircloth Amendment, which since 1998 has barred building any new public housing units, making future expansion legally possible for the first time in decades.

Grants residents formal power: elected resident councils in every project of 50 or more units, signed resident approval of grant applications, public hearings, and a resident vote on how surplus energy revenue is used.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the program — the bill appropriates 'such sums as necessary' to wipe out the public housing capital backlog plus ten years of spending, with no total price attached — meaning the general public bears the cost. Contractors taking on the work would also face strict wage, labor, and American-made materials requirements.

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates 'such sums as necessary' to eliminate the entire public housing capital backlog plus ten years of funding, an open-ended federal spending commitment with no price estimate in the bill itself.

Grant recipients must commit to never reducing the number of public housing units and to convert everything to zero-carbon homes within ten years, conditions that could strain smaller housing agencies or slow projects if funds or contractors are short.

Requirements like project labor agreements on large jobs and resident-approval of applications add administrative steps that critics say can raise construction costs and delay repairs, even though they aim to guarantee good wages and resident input.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits for residents — safe, efficient homes, training, jobs, water safety — are large and well targeted, and its labor and buy-American rules aim to make public spending build local careers. The main drawbacks are its enormous cost (an open-ended appropriation plus a $1 billion administration fund), strict rules such as the no-unit-reduction pledge and mandatory labor agreements that could slow projects or raise their price, and the administrative burden on small housing agencies. But since the bill has not advanced, these tradeoffs have not been tested in practice; the live cost today is only the forgone opportunity to fix a large repair backlog.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, and no further action has been taken since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on August 6, 2026 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services.
No committee markup, vote, or floor action has occurred since the referral; the bill's action history ends there.

The bill would fund grants to fix a public housing capital backlog, electrify and weatherize units, replace contaminated water pipes, and require that a growing share of jobs and contracts go to low-income residents and resident-owned businesses.
It would also repeal the Faircloth Amendment, the 1998 provision that bars the construction of new public housing units.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained yet, but the outcome so far — a referral with no movement — favors the status quo: aging public housing stays as it is, and the repair backlog remains unaddressed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the repair backlog persists

for.name: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Financial Services Committee.

for.name: 41 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all cosponsors are Democrats.

sides.party_line_note: All 41 cosponsors are House Democrats, and no Republicans have signed on; the bill was referred to committee and has drawn no Republican support.

industries.industry: Public housing residents (low- and very low-income households)
industries.note: Not an industry, but the directly affected group: residents gain renovated, healthier, cheaper-to-run homes, training, hiring preferences, and enforceable relocation protections.

industries.industry: Union construction and building-trades apprenticeship programs
industries.note: The bill channels massive retrofit spending through Davis-Bacon prevailing-wage contractors, requires project labor agreements on large projects, and mandates registered apprenticeship slots, a structural win for organized building trades.

industries.industry: Energy efficiency, heat pump, and solar installation industries
industries.note: Mandated all-electric retrofits, rooftop solar, storage, and smart systems across the entire public housing stock would create a large, guaranteed market for these firms and their workers.
The bill requires all materials to be American-made under Build America, Buy America rules and directs HUD to identify US-made products to buy at scale, directing demand to domestic manufacturers.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel heating and gas utility suppliers
industries.note: Electrification requirements replace gas stoves, water heaters, and furnaces in public housing, shrinking a market segment, while efficiency upgrades cut long-run energy purchases.

analysis.trajectory: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in August 2026 and has seen no action since; the committee's Republican majority controls whether anything moves. With no Republican cosponsors and a slim GOP House majority, the realistic path is that the bill sits in committee and dies when the Congress ends in January 2027, unless it is attached to a larger package.
